GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: The next stronger Pacific trough will approach the West Coast Monday, resulting in flow across the western CONUS turning southwesterly.
GJT.text:
High pressure remains in control through much of the weekend, keeping things dry and sunny. Temperatures remain on the cooler side through the weekend, with highs near to around 5 degrees below normal and seasonably cool lows. Across the northwest CO valleys, as well as the upper Colorado River Valley and CO Zone 23, subfreezing temperatures are once again forecast. A Freeze Warning is in effect through 9AM Saturday morning.

An area of low pressure that has been lurking off the SoCal coast the last few days is expected to become a mobile, open wave by Sunday, making its way toward the Four Corners. A bit of moisture a lift associated with the passing of this wave will result in some light mountain showers for the San Juans, generally in the form of rain. Some light snow showers will be possible Sunday night into Monday, but mainly at elevations above roughly 12k feet. Elsewhere, conditions remain dry.

The next stronger Pacific trough will approach the West Coast Monday, resulting in flow across the western CONUS turning southwesterly. This will begin to draw up rich tropical moisture through the Four Corners, leading to afternoon mountain showers where orographics are favorable, mainly across the San Juans and into the Central Divide Mountains. Better forcing looks to move in mid-week, as the Pacific low moves through SoCal and begins to track through the Desert Southwest. There is still a lot of uncertainty regarding this system, its exact track, timing, and strength. Suffice to say, it's looking like a return to cooler and unsettled weather is likely mid to late next week.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: By the latter half of the week, the chances for a more organized storm system increase. A strong cutoff low is expected to be centered over southern California by Thursday, which then shifts east towards Colorado by late week or sometime next weekend.
BOU.text:
We're off to a chilly start to the evening across the Platte River valley and some localized portions of the I-25 corridor. A few of our typical cold spots in the plains have already dipped below freezing, and a hard freeze is still expected across most of the northeastern plains overnight tonight. Temperatures should remain in the mid 30s to low 40s across most of the I-25 corridor, but there could be some patchy frost overnight.

Temperatures are expected to warm into the mid 70s across the plains on Saturday as the upper level ridge remains over the region. The airmass is exceptionally dry and it will be difficult to even muster a cloud during the day.

The ridge is expected to push off to the east by Sunday, as a weak cutoff low transitions back to an open wave, eventually drifting towards the forecast area under weak southwesterly flow. The only notable change in the weather will be an increase in cloud cover during the day Sunday, but temperatures are still expected to remain in the 70s.

That shortwave should move through our forecast area by Monday, bringing a slight chance of rain/snow showers to the higher terrain, while the plains remain mild and dry. A few showers could continue through mid-week with moisture lingering in the south- southwesterly flow aloft.

By the latter half of the week, the chances for a more organized storm system increase. A strong cutoff low is expected to be centered over southern California by Thursday, which then shifts east towards Colorado by late week or sometime next weekend. As is stands right now, the majority of deterministic and ensemble guidance keeps almost all of the meaningful precipitation to the south and west of our forecast area. Of course, this potential storm system is still about a week out, and it's likely we'll see shifts in the storm track over the next several days.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: If you are traveling across the Mountains Wednesday into Thursday, be prepared for heavy precipitation, and very high elevation snowfall. This area has seen heavy rainfall over the past month, and could be prone to flash flooding and slides.
PUB.text:
Good agreement between the various model solutions and ensembles through the extended period. The main concern through the extended period is a storm system slated for mid to late week impacting mountain areas.

Sunday through Tuesday...persistent southwest flow will prevail across southern Colorado into early next week. Two upper waves embedded in the flow will lead to isolated to scattered mountains showers and thunderstorms. Dry conditions will prevail on Sunday as upper energy begins to lift out of Arizona. Sunday temperatures will be warm, with mostly lower to mid 70s across the Plains. An isolated shower may be possible across the San Juan Range by late Sunday afternoon as energy approaches.

The upper energy over Arizona will track northeast across Colorado on Monday. Expected shower coverage to increase across the Continental Divide Sunday night and continue through Monday afternoon. Not much cold air with this energy, and snow levels will be high, above 12-13 kft. A quick inch or two may be possible above these elevations across the San Juans. As the upper wave tracks northeast, a few showers may spread northeast into Teller County and the Palmer Divide Monday evening. Not much moisture to work with unfavorable southwest flow aloft will likely limit precipitation to just a few light showers if anything at all. The Plains look to remain dry as this energy moves northeast.

By Tuesday, an upper low moves into the West Coast with moisture moving northward out of the tropics. This will help prime the area for the upper storm system for mid to late week. A few light showers will remain possible along the Continental Divide Tuesday due to persistent southwest flow and embedded energy.

A weak boundary will arrive on Monday, knocking 3 to 5 degrees off highs Monday afternoon. Temperatures will rebound on Tuesday back into the lower to mid 70s across the Plains.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Mostly benign conditions to start the work week in the long term, but this pattern should begin to be broken up by a deep Pacific system that will encroach our region by the end of the forecast period.
CYS.text: Mostly benign conditions to start the work week in the long term, but this pattern should begin to be broken up by a deep Pacific system that will encroach our region by the end of the forecast period. Monday starts with high pressure ridging mostly holding control of our forecast area, but a weakening upper level low will move across the Four Corners region and then just to our southeast through Tuesday afternoon. While mostly non- impactful, this feature will at least bring a very low end chance of some high elevation precipitation, along with a small bump in moisture. This influx of moisture will continue through the rest of the week as our upper level flow turns southwesterly while we sit between high pressure controlling the southeastern US and a deep Pacific system that will move inland by later Wednesday into Thursday. This feature will be the next noteworthy system to impact the forecast area as we see precipitation begin overspreading late Thursday into Friday and start another cooling trend that should persist into the weekend. For this forecast period, expect mostly similar temperatures day to day as highs will be around 6 to 12 degrees above normal, generally in the 60's to 70's, with lows similarly warm in the 40's. Any drop in temperatures would occur just beyond the long term after the Pacific system moves in, and the most impactful precipitation chances similarly just beyond this forecast time as well. Overall it should be a quiet period, but that will be ending by the weekend after next.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: - Snow levels look to remain above 9000-9500 feet through Friday morning, falling to near 8000-8500 feet by Friday evening. Total snow accumulations above 9500 feet will be 4 to 8 inches or so by Friday evening.
SLC.text:
- Isolated showers and thunderstorms will return far southern Utah late Sunday morning into Sunday evening.

- More widespread precipitation will develop Wednesday morning and impact much of the region. Most areas will see between 0.50 and 1.50 inches of precipitation by Friday evening, with locally higher amounts in excess of 2.00 inches.

- Snow levels look to remain above 9000-9500 feet through Friday morning, falling to near 8000-8500 feet by Friday evening. Total snow accumulations above 9500 feet will be 4 to 8 inches or so by Friday evening.

BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Ensemble guidance largely favors another cold front late Thursday into Friday as another upper-level trough moves into the Pacific NW and BC, Canada. This feature will have the low rejoin the broader flow and move east through the day Friday.
BOI.text:
Through much of the work week, the upper-level low pressure system will move from just off the California coast to lingering in the Great Basin. Temperatures will cool off Tuesday as another weak front moves into the region along with increasing cloud cover during the day. Models are split on fully moving the front through the area or having it stall out in southwest ID. Regardless, temperatures will cool down to near- normal in southeast OR and around 5 degrees above normal in southwest ID. Flow aloft through much of the week will be out of the south, gradually increasing PWATs through at least Thursday. This, along with favorable topographic effects, will introduce widespread precipitation chances Wednesday afternoon into Thursday.

Ensemble guidance largely favors another cold front late Thursday into Friday as another upper-level trough moves into the Pacific NW and BC, Canada. This feature will have the low rejoin the broader flow and move east through the day Friday. This will lead to even colder temperatures going into next weekend. The synoptic pattern with the next trough is too uncertain to discuss Saturday any further at this time.
